# Memory curation

Propose every change and wait for the user's confirmation before you delete, supersede or update a memory; never run this unattended. Present the proposals as a short list with each memory's id and title.

1. **Status.** Call `memory_status` and keep its counts by state and kind for the end.
2. **Hypotheses.** `memory_list` with `state: "hypothesis"`; read each with `memory_get`. Propose to keep it (a `used` verdict through `memory_feedback` brings it back), correct it with `memory_update` or delete it with `memory_delete`.
3. **Duplicates.** For each hypothesis and each memory on the listed pages, `memory_search` its title; it finds active and hypothesis memories alike. A different memory that teaches the same lesson is a duplicate. Propose one merge per pair: keep the more complete one (an active one before a hypothesis), fold anything only the other says into it with `memory_update`, then `memory_delete` the other; for a changed single-valued fact use `memory_store` with resolution `SUPERSEDE` instead.
4. **Stale facts.** `memory_list` with `kind: "fact"`, newest first; pass `next_cursor` as `before` for the next page. A changed value is a `memory_store` with resolution `SUPERSEDE`; a fact that no longer holds is a `memory_delete`.
5. **Wrong scope.** Scope and kind cannot change in place: store the memory again with the right scope or kind (`memory_store`), then delete the old one (`memory_delete`).
6. **Recall keys.** Fix keywords and anchors with `memory_update`, following [the authoring standard](../memory/references/authoring.md) (`memory/references/authoring.md`); each replaces the stored value whole. A memory without `questions` is found less often: propose 3–6, in English and in the user's language, and add them with `memory_update`.
7. **Before and after.** Call `memory_status` again and report both sets of counts.

A memory that `memory_list` finds only with `project: "all"` belongs to another project: it is read-only here and can be changed only from a session in its own project.

# Memory capture

One local database serves every project. Hook recall and `memory_search` surface memories automatically; you are the only author, and storing is always your decision.

## When to store, and what

| Moment | Store |
|---|---|
| The user corrects how you work | A `pattern` right away, before continuing: the rule and the reason. |
| The user asks you to remember something | That fact or rule, now. |
| You inferred a non-obvious project convention | The convention and the evidence for it. |
| You solved a problem | The reasoning a future session cannot read from the diff: why this approach, what was rejected, which constraint forced it. Not the fix itself. |

Rules for every memory:

- Store only what a future session could not re-derive from the code, git history or the project's always-loaded instruction file. The server rejects content that restates a line of the instruction files it reads.
- English, one topic per memory, insight first, then the reason.
- Searchable terms: file paths, module names, commands, error signatures.
- `questions`: 3–6 short prompts a user would type when this memory matters — the task or the symptom, not the answer (`How do I run the billing tests?`, `pytest fails with too many connections`). Write them in English and in the language the user writes in. Recall compares every prompt with each question, so they are how a memory is found in any language.
- Do not ask the user before saving. Do not store agent, task or system text: write the lesson in your own words.

The hooks never store anything and never flag a correction or a remember request: notice those yourself, in any language, and store them right away. After a failing command later passed, the Stop hook returns a memory checkpoint when you finish the turn without a store: store the durable lesson, or say there is none, then finish.

## Acting on recall

Recalled constraints start with `Apply —`, procedures with `Follow —`. Apply or follow each one, or say why it does not apply. Then call `memory_feedback` once per turn with a verdict on every injected id, each id in one list: `used` when it informed the work, `not_applicable` when it was irrelevant here, `wrong` when it was incorrect or outdated — for example `{used: [id1], not_applicable: [id2, id3]}`. An id you leave out counts as no evidence either way. A `wrong` memory leaves recall until a `used` verdict or a store of the same content brings it back; nothing is deleted.

## The slot every store names

- `type`: `semantic` facts, `procedural` how-tos, `episodic` events, `pattern` corrections and preferences.
- `scope=user` only for what holds across projects (the user, their tools); `scope=project` otherwise.
- `kind`: `constraint`, `preference`, `fact`, `procedure` or `belief`.
- `conflict_key`: a stable lowercase dotted key, the same every time the same question is answered — `project.primary_database`, `test.command.backend`, `team.reviewers`.
- `cardinality`: `single` when the slot holds one current value, `multi` when several coexist.
- `value_text`: the slot's value in a few words (`PostgreSQL 15`); required for `single`.
- `keywords` and `anchors` help recall find it. Before a tool call a memory is recalled only when an anchor matches exactly: before Bash, a command head (`pytest`, `git commit`); before Read, Edit or Write, a project-relative path or basename (`billing/tax.py`), a directory prefix ending in `/` (`migrations/versions/`) or an extension starting with `.` (`.vue`) of the file.
- A lesson tied to a ticket: put the ticket id, upper-case as it appears in the branch (`TOUCH-4945`), into both `keywords` and `anchors`. Session start on a branch that carries the ticket then recalls it.
- A lesson about an error: put its stable tokens — the code, class name or module name (`SQLITE_BUSY`, `ModuleNotFoundError`, `express`) — into `anchors`. A failing Bash command recalls it only through an anchor equal to a token of its error, once per session and command; keywords are not matched there, and a command head alone never recalls it.

## Authoring standard

Read [memory/references/authoring.md](references/authoring.md) before you write or edit a memory: it gives each field's limit and form, the namespaces a `conflict_key` may start with, and the anchor forms recall can match, with good and bad examples.
The server rejects an anchor or key that no recall path can hit and names the fix; correct that field and repeat the call.

## When the answer is needs_resolution

The server wrote nothing and lists the candidates it found, active ones and hypotheses alike; each names its `state`. Repeat the same call with `resolution`:

- `SUPERSEDE` + `target` — a single-valued fact changed; the old memory is revoked.
- `UPDATE` + `target` — refine the same fact in place.
- `NOOP` + `target` — it is already known; only its support count changes.
- `ADD` — a genuinely different memory.

A rejection message names the resolution to use instead. An exact duplicate of an active or hypothesis memory is recorded as `noop` automatically, and a hypothesis comes back to active. When a candidate in `hypothesis` holds the lesson you are storing, `NOOP` or `UPDATE` it instead of `ADD`: that brings it back to active rather than leaving a copy beside it; `SUPERSEDE` targets active memories only.

## Reading and curating

- Recall shows abstracts with the full id; read the body with `memory_get`.
- Hook recall injects active memories only; `memory_search` also finds memories in `hypothesis` and names each result's `state`.
- `memory_list` browses memories newest first, without content, filtered by state, kind, type or scope; pass its `next_cursor` as `before` for the next page. `project: "all"` shows every project's memories, read-only.
- `memory_update` edits title, abstract, content, keywords or anchors, and questions in place; keywords, anchors and questions replace the stored value whole. Revoked memories are immutable, and scope or kind cannot change: store the memory again, then delete the old one. Importance is derived from feedback, never typed.
- For a full review with the user, use the `memory-curate` skill.
- `memory_relate` is for load-bearing connections only, at most 20 per memory.
- `memory_status` shows what the memory holds and does for this project: counts, the recall switch, how often recall injects, open capture moments and the last injections.
- The user can switch recall off for this project; storing keeps working while it is off.
- If recall reports a degraded mode or a session-start notice says memory is off, run the memory doctor and follow the fix it names.

# Adaptive cognitive memory

Gives Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode one local memory shared by every project: what the agent stores in one session comes back in later sessions, on any of the three hosts. Memory content never leaves your machine.

## Install

You need Node.js ≥ 22. On Claude Code, run:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add d2a8k3u/adaptive-cognitive-memory
claude plugin install adaptive-cognitive-memory@adaptive-cognitive-memory
```

Codex and OpenCode need a few more steps (dependencies, the MCP server entry, and on Codex the hook review): follow [Install](docs/install.md#install).

The first session downloads the embedding model (about 120 MB) in the background. Then check the install with `/memory-doctor` on Claude Code, or with the doctor line from [Commands and CLI](docs/cli.md) on Codex and OpenCode. It rates every check `ok`, `warn` or `fail` and gives the fix for each one that is not ok.

On Claude Code, uninstalling the plugin from the last scope it is installed at deletes the store until you move it. Export or move the store first: [Uninstall](docs/install.md#uninstall).

## How it works

Every project, on every host, reads and writes one `memory.sqlite` in the shared data directory, `$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory` by default ([Storage](docs/storage.md#layout)). An existing Claude Code store stays where it is until you move it with one command ([Move the Claude Code store](docs/storage.md#move-the-claude-code-store)).

A memory has a scope, `project` (visible only in that project) or `user` (visible everywhere), and a type: `semantic` (facts), `procedural` (how-tos), `episodic` (session events) or `pattern` (lessons and preferences). Memories are stored in English. Each one carries recall questions in English and in the user's language, and the local embedding model is multilingual, so prompts in other languages find them.

Recall is automatic. Hooks inject one-line abstracts under a token budget at session start, on every prompt, before tool calls and after a failed Bash command. The agent reads a memory's full body with `memory_get`.

Capture is explicit: nothing is saved automatically. The agent stores durable knowledge with the `memory_*` MCP tools, guided by the bundled `memory` skill. It notices a correction or a remember request itself, in any language; the hooks only point at a failing command that later passed. A store that finds related memories writes nothing and returns them, and the agent decides to supersede, update, skip or add. Superseded memories stay readable but never reach recall.

No outbound request carries memory content: the MCP server talks stdio only and the hooks make no LLM calls. The one network operation is the one-time model download. Secrets are redacted when a memory is stored and again on export.

A broken part is never silent. Without the embedding model or the sqlite-vec extension, recall falls back to FTS5 keyword search with a visible warning. A native module that does not load, or a database written by a newer plugin version, turns memory off with one notice at session start. The doctor names the broken piece and its fix.

## Host differences

Codex has no failure capture, no recall after a failed command and no statusline badge. OpenCode appends pre-tool recall after the tool call and has no statusline badge. Both run the commands as CLI lines instead of slash commands. The full matrix is in [Install](docs/install.md).

# Contributing

## Set up

```bash
git clone git@github.com:d2a8k3u/adaptive-cognitive-memory.git
cd adaptive-cognitive-memory
npm ci
```

[Development](docs/development.md) lists where everything lives, the checks, the performance gates and the evals.

## Make a change

1. Create a branch from `main`.
2. Run `npm run check` until it passes. If you touched `src/`, run `npm run build` and commit the updated `dist/`.
3. If you changed the recall or hook path, check the [performance gates](docs/development.md#performance-gates) on your machine.
4. Commit with [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/): `type(scope): description`.
5. Open a pull request.

## Code style

- TypeScript strict mode, CommonJS output, Node ≥ 22.
- Biome enforces formatting: 2-space indent, 100-column lines, double quotes, LF, organized imports.
- No comments. Names and structure carry the meaning; rationale belongs in the commit message.
- No `any`. Use `unknown` and narrow it.
- Never weaken a test to make a change pass; the tests define the contract.

## Report an issue

Open an issue with:

- what you expected and what happened
- steps to reproduce, including the shape of the memory content (never real secrets)
- Node.js version and OS
- the doctor output: `/memory-doctor` on Claude Code, the doctor line from [Commands and CLI](docs/cli.md) on Codex and OpenCode

# Capture

Nothing is saved automatically. The agent stores durable knowledge with the `memory_*` MCP tools, guided by the bundled `memory` skill. It notices a correction or a remember request itself, in any language; the hooks only point at a failing command that later passed.

## Two-phase store

Every memory names its slot (`kind`, `conflict_key`, `cardinality`, `value_text`). A store that finds related active or hypothesis memories in its project (same key, nearest vectors, keyword hits) writes nothing and returns them as `needs_resolution`, each with its `state`. The agent repeats the call with `SUPERSEDE`, `UPDATE`, `NOOP` or `ADD`, and the server rejects a resolution that would break a single-valued key or cross a project. Superseded memories are revoked: they stay readable but never reach recall. A procedure, constraint or preference with the same key and value in two projects is copied to `user` scope; facts never are.

## Capture moments and the Stop checkpoint

- A Bash command that failed and later passed in the same session opens a resolution moment.
- When a turn ends with such a moment still open (no `memory_store` or `memory_update` since), the Stop hook returns one memory checkpoint: store the durable lesson, or say there is none, then finish. It never fires while a stop hook is already continuing the turn.
- `memory_feedback` verdicts drive the lifecycle. The PostToolUse hook records each call's verdict per id for its session. A memory used in fewer than half of at least 5 sessions that gave it an explicit verdict becomes a `hypothesis`: hook recall leaves it out, while `memory_search` and the store still find it. A session that gave the memory no verdict counts neither way, however often it was injected. A `wrong` verdict demotes at once. Constraints and preferences are pinned into every session start whatever the task, so their used share says nothing about their worth: they leave recall only on a `wrong` verdict. A memory that returns to active starts a fresh trial, in which only verdicts given after its return count. Nothing is deleted.

## Hook output

All hooks run `dist/hooks.js`, always exit 0 and never block. They print at most one JSON object: `{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"<event>","additionalContext":"…"}}`, or, at session start when the database cannot be used, `{"systemMessage":"…"}` naming the cause and the fix. While the embedding model is missing, session start adds a `systemMessage` beside the context: the model is downloading, or, with `download_model` off, run the doctor. After a failed download the message names the failure's first line (at most 120 characters) and says the download is retrying. When no download is running, that session start also launches `model-init` as a detached background process and does not wait for it; no other event starts one. Any other internal failure prints one class-only line to stderr and nothing to stdout.

# Commands and CLI

Every host runs the same CLI, `node <root>/dist/cli.js <command>`. `<root>` is the plugin root: the checkout, or on Codex the plugin cache directory of the installed version (see [Install](install.md#codex)). Claude Code also wraps three of the commands as slash commands; on Codex and OpenCode, run the lines below from a shell.

Every line sets `ACM_DATA_DIR`, the shared store: `$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory` unless you chose another (see [Configuration](configuration.md#environment-variables)). `recall` works on the project of the working directory, so run it from inside that project.

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `doctor` | JSON health report; exit 1 when a check fails |
| `recall on\|off` | recall switch for the project of the working directory |
| `statusline on\|off` | Claude Code only. Opt-in statusline badge: `on` installs the shim and prints the line for your statusline script, `off` removes the plugin's statusline files and prints the line to remove; neither touches any `settings.json` (see [Statusline badge](statusline.md)) |
| `store move --from <dir>` | moves the Claude Code store into the shared data directory (see [Store move](#store-move) and [Storage](storage.md#move-the-claude-code-store)) |
| `export <file>` | writes JSONL: a header, then one record per memory, relation and transition. A memory record holds every column needed to restore it, state, counters and timestamps included, but no vector. Secrets are redacted again, personal data is kept. Refuses an existing file; stamps the export time the doctor reads |
| `import <file>` | validates every line first and rejects the whole file naming each bad line; every memory must pass the same key rules as `memory_store` (conflict key, value, keywords, anchors), except that a legacy empty `conflict_key` (`""`) is kept; then writes in one transaction. A memory id already present is skipped (re-import is a no-op); an active single-valued memory whose slot another active memory holds, or a memory with more than 20 relations, rejects the import naming the line. Imported text is redacted like a stored memory's. Imported rows arrive without vectors: run `reembed` (each server start embeds up to 32 active ones) |
| `model-init` | one-time model download, the only command that touches the network (session start runs it in the background unless `download_model` is off). It downloads into a staging directory beside the model cache and moves the finished model into place, so an interrupted download never leaves a partial model; a lock in the data directory admits one download at a time (exit 1 while another runs; a lock older than 15 minutes is taken over), and a failure is recorded for the doctor. Prints the model's size and path; does nothing when the model is already cached |
| `reembed` | realigns vector states that drifted while sqlite-vec was not loaded, then embeds every memory still missing a vector (the MCP server does both for up to 32 active ones after it connects; a failure there leaves the rows unembedded and shows in the doctor's `unembedded` check) |

# Configuration

## Plugin options

The three options have the same names, defaults and bounds on every host:

| Option | Meaning | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `recall_budget_tokens` | injection budget, SessionStart + UserPromptSubmit | `1200` | 100–2375 |
| `pretool_budget_tokens` | injection budget, PreToolUse and PostToolUseFailure | `300` | 100–2375 |

## Native auto memory (Claude Code)

Claude Code's own auto memory (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md`, or the `autoMemoryDirectory` setting) is on by default and can run beside this plugin. The plugin reads the same settings Claude Code does: `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY` (`1` off, `0` on) first, then `autoMemoryEnabled` in `.claude/settings.local.json`, `.claude/settings.json` and `~/.claude/settings.json`, highest first. It cannot see managed settings or `--settings`, so the doctor qualifies its verdict with "as far as the readable settings show". While auto memory is on:

- SessionStart (`startup`, `clear`, `compact`) adds one line asking Claude to store durable lessons with `memory_store`, not in `MEMORY.md`.
- `memory_store` rejects content that restates a line of that `MEMORY.md` (as it does for `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/*.md`).
- The doctor warns (`auto_memory`). To make this plugin the only durable memory, set `"autoMemoryEnabled": false` in `.claude/settings.json` (one project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (every project).

On Codex and OpenCode the plugin ignores native auto memory.

## Real-session eval

`evals/` holds a `claude plugin eval` suite that runs a real model against the plugin. It checks that a correction, a remember request and a resolved failure lead to a store; that a conflicting fact goes through the two-phase store and supersedes the old value; that a content-free prompt, a neutral turn and another project's fact inject nothing; and that a superseded fact and a pre-tool procedure reach the answer. Each case's scaffold links the embedding model cached by `npm test` into the run's plugin data directory and seeds memories through the real MCP server. The cases need the real server and Bash:

```bash
claude plugin eval . --tag baseline --ablation with-without --mocks off --scaffold \
  --allow-tools "mcp__plugin_adaptive-cognitive-memory_memory__*" Bash --trust-plugin

  --allow-tools "mcp__plugin_adaptive-cognitive-memory_memory__*" Bash --trust-plugin
```

Transcripts carry only SessionStart hook output, so whether a memory was injected is checked in each run's database (`--keep-temp`, then the `injections` and `session_signals` tables), not with trace graders.

## Embedding model

The first session downloads the embedding model once, into the store's data directory: `onnx-community/granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2-ONNX`, int8, about 120 MB. It is the only network operation the plugin performs, and it never carries memory content. The download runs in the background, so the session starts at once with a notice. Until it finishes, prompts recall nothing (session-start and pre-tool recall need no model), `memory_search` matches keywords only, and new memories are stored without a vector; the next memory server start embeds up to 32 of them and `reembed` embeds the rest. A failed download is retried at every session start, and that session's notice names the failure.

To keep the plugin off the network, turn the download off and cache the model yourself. On Claude Code, turn the `download_model` option off (`/config`, or `claude plugin configure adaptive-cognitive-memory`); on Codex and OpenCode, set `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_DOWNLOAD_MODEL=false` in the environment (see [Configuration](configuration.md)). Then cache the model:

```bash
ACM_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory" node "<root>/dist/cli.js" model-init
```

Then run the doctor ([Commands and CLI](cli.md)). It prints a JSON health report; exit code 1 means a check failed. Its `model` check shows a running download, the last failed one, and the command above with the paths filled in.

# Recall

Hooks inject one-line abstracts under a token budget at session start, on every user prompt, before tool calls and after a failed Bash command. The agent reads a memory's full body with `memory_get` and the full id on the recalled line.

## What the agent sees

The injection holds abstracts only, never content. Tokens are estimated as characters / 4, and an injection never exceeds 9,500 characters whatever the budget, because the host truncates additional context above 10,000:

```
Native auto memory is also on: store durable lessons with memory_store, not in the auto-memory MEMORY.md.
memory degraded (model missing) — run /memory-doctor
<memory>
Recalled memory from earlier sessions; verify it against the current code. Apply or follow each line, or say why it does not apply, then send memory_feedback for every id.
Constraints:
- Apply — release only from the main branch (valid from 2026-10-13 · project · 01K7Q3M5X8R2C9V4N6B1T0ZJHD)
Preferences:
- prefer pnpm for new TypeScript projects (valid from 2026-10-02 · user · 01K6ZP2Y7W3N8D5Q1F4H9GX0RB)
Project facts:
- deploys go to the ECS cluster (valid from 2026-10-10 · project · 01K7JD9C4T6M1Q8W2Z5R3N7BXA)
Procedures:
- Follow — run uv run pytest -q from the repository root (valid from 2026-10-11 · project · 01K7MA0F3H8B6Y2K9V1D4S7CWE)
</memory>
```

The first line appears only on Claude Code, at session start while native auto memory is on. The second appears only when a prompt's recall ran degraded. Empty sections are left out. Constraints start with `Apply —`, procedures with `Follow —`.

## When recall runs

| Event | Behaviour | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| `SessionStart` | the active constraints and preferences of the user and the project, ranked by derived importance, then rows injected fewer than 500 injection events ago, then recency; on a branch carrying a ticket id then up to 3 rows keyed with it (see below); on `resume` and `compact` also every row injected earlier in the session | `recall_budget_tokens` (1200) |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | admission, then KNN over each memory's vector and its recall questions plus FTS5 candidates, then the prompt gate (see [Prompt recall](#prompt-recall)); at most 3 rows, best score first | `recall_budget_tokens` (1200) |
| `PreToolUse` (`Bash\|Edit\|Write\|Read`) | no embedding: the Bash command head (`pytest`, `git commit`, `uv run pytest` → also `pytest`) and the project paths its arguments name with their directory prefixes (`go test ./internal/it/...` → `internal/it/`), or the read or edited path (relative path, basename, directory prefixes, extensions) matched exactly against each memory's anchors | `pretool_budget_tokens` (300) |
| `PostToolUseFailure` (`Bash`) | no embedding: terms of the redacted error text matched exactly against each memory's anchors, once per session and command head (see below) | `pretool_budget_tokens` (300) |

Rows already injected in the session since its latest SessionStart are skipped. Dedup scope, observed 2026-10-20: subagent hooks carry the parent's `session_id`, so a row injected in the parent is skipped inside a subagent.

## Prompt recall

Admission comes first: slash commands and prompts with fewer than 3 distinct words of two or more letters inject nothing and never load the model. No word list decides what counts, and text in scripts written without spaces, such as Japanese or Chinese, is split into words first.

A memory's cosine is the better of its own vector's and its best recall question's. One gate serves every language: a calibrated linear score must reach the frozen threshold. The score combines the cosine, its gap to the best candidate, its gap to the mean of the prompt's 10 nearest memories (a sparse store fills the missing ones with a calibrated background cosine), the BM25 strength, whether the memory is the best candidate, and whether its key or keywords match the prompt. Beliefs and unverified rows also need a key hit.

The gate is fitted, not hand-tuned: `npm run eval:fit` stores the eval corpus through the real memory server, collects every calibration prompt's candidates the way the hook does (240 positive and 207 negative prompts in English and Czech), fits a logistic model on them and picks the threshold with the most gold hits whose false-injection rate stays within 3%; the weights, threshold and background cosine live in `src/calibration.ts`, and a test pins the record to the live embedding model and its query, passage and question inputs. On the held-out confirmation split (240 positive, 120 negative prompts) the fitted gate reaches a gold hit of 57.5%, precision 82.1% and false injections 2/120; prompts in German, Spanish, Polish and Japanese are measured by the `recall_multilingual` eval suite and never used for fitting.

An embedding run has a 1.5 s deadline per event (`ACM_EMBED_DEADLINE_MS`). Without a query vector, `UserPromptSubmit` injects only the degraded warning, which names `embedding timeout` when the deadline passed and `model missing` when the model failed.

## Events per host

The table above names Claude Code's events. Codex and OpenCode run the same recall from their own events:

| Recall | Claude Code | Codex | OpenCode |
|---|---|---|---|
| session start | `SessionStart` | `SessionStart` | the first `chat.message` of a session; `experimental.session.compacting` recalls again after a compaction |
| every prompt | `UserPromptSubmit` | `UserPromptSubmit` | `chat.message` |
| before a tool call | `PreToolUse` | `PreToolUse` | none: recall for the tool is appended after the call, from `tool.execute.after` |
| after a failed Bash command | `PostToolUseFailure` | none | `tool.execute.after` of `bash`, failure read from `metadata.exit` |
| Stop checkpoint | `Stop` | `Stop`, answered as `{"decision":"block","reason":…}` whose reason becomes the continuation prompt | `session.idle`, answered by a re-prompt through the plugin's client |

Codex gives its hooks no exit status for a Bash command, so Codex has no failure capture and no failure recall, and `resolution` signals stay inert. On OpenCode the injected text is added as a text part of the message. The recall header names the bare `memory_feedback`, the server's own tool name; each host prefixes it as listed in [MCP tools and skills](tools.md).

Texts that tell you to run the doctor name the host's form: `/memory-doctor` on Claude Code, and on Codex and OpenCode the `node <root>/dist/cli.js doctor` line from [Commands and CLI](cli.md).

## Turning recall off

`recall off` turns recall off for the current project (its git repository, or its directory outside git). The hooks inject no memories there, while capture, the Stop checkpoint, `memory_store` and `memory_search` keep working. `recall on` turns it back on. On Claude Code run `/memory-recall off` or `/memory-recall on`; on Codex and OpenCode run the `recall on|off` line from [Commands and CLI](cli.md) inside the project.

## Branch-aware session start

Session start reads the current branch inside the `git rev-parse` call that already resolves the project (`--git-common-dir --git-dir`, then the `HEAD` file of the git dir), so no git process is added. The ticket id is the first token of 2–10 letters or digits, a hyphen and 1–6 digits in the branch name, upper-cased: `fix/TOUCH-4945/guide-list-search` and `fix/touch-4945-x` both give `TOUCH-4945`. Words of the branch name are never used. When there is a ticket, up to 3 memories of the project and the user are added after the pinned constraints and preferences and before the rows carried over on `resume` and `compact`, the most important first, within the same budget and the same SessionStart recall event. A memory matches only when one of its anchors equals the ticket id or its keywords hold it as a phrase (`TOUCH-4945` or `touch 4945`); `touch` alone or `TOUCH-49450` never match, and another project's memories never do. A version-like name such as `release-2026` reads as the ticket `RELEASE-2026` and matches only memories keyed with exactly that id. On `main`, a detached HEAD, outside git or when git fails, session start is unchanged. A repository on the reftable ref format keeps no branch in its `HEAD` file, so it gets no ticket rows. In a repository whose path holds a newline the two-line answer is ambiguous, so one more `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` resolves the project to the same id, and it gets no ticket rows. To make a lesson come back on its ticket's branch, put the ticket id, upper-case as it appears in the branch, into both `keywords` and `anchors`.

## Recall on a failed Bash command

When a Bash command fails (`PostToolUseFailure`, not an interrupt), the hook takes signature terms from the error text Claude Code passes, redacted first and cut to its first 500 characters, at most 32 of them: error class names (`TypeError`, `ModuleNotFoundError`), upper-case codes (`ENOENT`, `SQLITE_BUSY`, `ECONNREFUSED`, `E401`), the module name after `Cannot find module`, `No module named` or `could not resolve`, and path basenames (`tax.py`). The `Exit code N` line, `:line:col` suffixes, hex runs of 7 or more, durations, timestamps, absolute path prefixes, colour codes, the redaction marker and status words such as `ERROR`, `ERR`, `FAIL` or `PASS` never become terms. A visible memory is injected only when one of its anchors equals a term; its conflict key and keywords are not matched on this path, and the command head alone never admits a row, so a memory anchored only on `pytest` comes back after a failing `pytest` only when the error text itself names `pytest`. Recall runs once per session and command head: the first failure of `pytest` that injects something uses up `pytest` for the rest of the session, even after it passes, while a failure that injects nothing leaves it unused. It shares the PreToolUse budget (`pretool_budget_tokens`), skips rows already injected since the session's latest start, does nothing while recall is off and loads no model. The error text is never stored; only the command head is, for the resolution moment. To make a lesson come back on its error, put the code, class name or module name into `anchors`.

# Statusline badge (Claude Code only)

The badge shows in your Claude Code statusline how many memories the session injected and when recall last ran. Codex and OpenCode have no statusline badge.

The badge is one line of at most 40 characters, `mem <n> · last <event> <hh:mm>` (the distinct memories injected in this session, the last recall event and its local time), or `mem off` while recall is off for the project.

## Turn it on

The badge is opt-in: until you run `/memory-statusline on`, no hook or command writes a statusline file. `on` installs a small shim and an enabled marker in `<plugin data dir>/statusline/` and prints one line for your own statusline command; the badge never reads or writes any `settings.json`.

`<plugin data dir>` stands for the store's data directory: the shared directory after the [store move](storage.md#move-the-claude-code-store), or `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` before it. The line the command prints carries the real path.

Used alone as the `statusLine` command, the line works as printed:

```bash
{ test -f "<plugin data dir>/statusline/badge.cjs" && node "<plugin data dir>/statusline/badge.cjs"; } || :
```

In a script that reads the statusline's stdin once (`input="$(cat)"`) and hands it to several commands, replay it into the line:

```bash
printf '%s' "$input" | { test -f "<plugin data dir>/statusline/badge.cjs" && node "<plugin data dir>/statusline/badge.cjs"; } || :
```

## What it reads and writes

While the badge is on, each recall hook (session start, prompt, pre-tool) writes its session's badge state to `<plugin data dir>/statusline/`: one file per session, replaced atomically, so a reader never sees a torn file. Session start prunes state files older than 30 days and reinstalls the shim after a plugin update.

The shim reads only node built-ins and its own files, never the database. It prints nothing and exits 0 when there is nothing to show: badge off, unknown session, missing or unreadable state, malformed stdin.

## Turn it off

`/memory-statusline off` stops the writes, removes `<plugin data dir>/statusline/` and prints the same line for you to remove.

The store move prints the `statusLine` command for the new shim path when the badge is on. Set it, because the shim path changes with the data directory.

Before the move, uninstalling deletes the plugin data directory, so before you uninstall, run `/memory-statusline off` and remove the line from your statusline script.

# Storage

One SQLite database (WAL, `busy_timeout` 5000 ms, short immediate transactions) holds:

- `memories`: ulid id, type, kind, scope, `project_id`, title, abstract, content, slot, state, counters, derived importance ((1 + used) / (2 + used + failures) with failures = 2 × wrong + receipted injections without use), the start of its current trial (when it last became active), validity timestamps. `project_id` is the first 16 hex chars of the sha256 of the project's git common dir, so every subdirectory and worktree of one repository shares it; outside git it hashes the directory's real path.
- `relations` (explicit, capped at 20 per source), `memories_vec` (sqlite-vec, float[384] cosine over title, content and keywords, with a `state` column so KNN filters to active rows), `questions_vec` (one vector per recall question, with the memory's scope, project and state so KNN filters inside the query), `memories_fts` (FTS5 over title, abstract, conflict key, keywords and value).
- `transitions`: every supersession, promotion, demotion and reactivation with its evidence.
- `verdicts`: every explicit `used`, `not_applicable` or `wrong` verdict with its session and time, the evidence the lifecycle decides on.
- `injections`, `receipt_sessions`, `recall_events`: what each session was shown, which sessions gave receipts, and one row per recall hook run with the number of rows it injected (kept to the newest 10,000 at each session start).
- `session_signals`, `command_failures`: capture moments. `failure_recalls`: the session and command heads whose failure already injected. Session start drops closed signals, command failures and failure recalls older than 30 days.
- `project_settings`: the per-project recall switch.

Concurrent sessions are safe: an externally locked database surfaces an explicit `database locked` error, never a partial write. The database records the embedding model's identity and dimension. Opening a database embedded by another model or dimension drops its vectors, keeps every memory and records the live model; the next memory server start (or `reembed`) embeds them again. Every open stamps the plugin version that wrote the database. A database whose schema is newer than the running plugin supports is refused with both versions named and "update the plugin".

## Layout

All three hosts read and write one store in the shared data directory: `ACM_DATA_DIR`, by default `$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory` (see [Configuration](configuration.md#environment-variables)). It holds:

- `memory.sqlite` with its `-wal` and `-shm` files, the database described above;
- `models/`, the cached embedding model;
- `statusline/`, the Claude Code badge files, only while the badge is on (see [Statusline badge](statusline.md));
- `.moving/`, staging for a [store move](#move-the-claude-code-store), on the same filesystem as the final path.

The directory is created with owner-only permissions. Nothing in it is host-specific, so a memory stored from one host is recalled on the others.

## Move the Claude Code store

A Claude Code install made before the shared directory existed keeps its store in its plugin data directory. Claude Code reads and writes that legacy store until you move it: nothing is created in the shared directory beforehand, and each session start, the MCP server's instructions, `memory_status` and the doctor's `plugin_data` check show a notice with the move command. Codex and OpenCode use the shared directory from the start, so they do not see the legacy memories before the move.

The move never runs by itself. Before you run it, install this plugin version and quit every Claude Code session, then run it from a terminal. If you also want Codex, move before you install on Codex; otherwise Codex creates a fresh store and the move refuses (see [An existing store in the shared directory](#an-existing-store-in-the-shared-directory)).

```bash
ACM_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory" node "<root>/dist/cli.js" store move --from "$HOME/.claude/plugins/data/adaptive-cognitive-memory-adaptive-cognitive-memory"
```

The command copies the database into a staging directory under `.moving/`, verifies the copy, publishes it into the shared directory and only then marks the legacy directory. It never writes the legacy store: the only file it adds there is `moved.json` (`{"version":1,"movedTo":…,"movedAt":…,"digest":…}`). The exit lines are listed in [Commands and CLI](cli.md#store-move). If the Claude Code statusline badge is on, the success output also prints the `statusLine` command to set for the new path. Restart Claude Code afterwards; Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode then share the store.

The move holds the legacy database's write lock from the copy to the marker, then releases it without writing. It does not fence tool calls that are in flight or start during that hold, a vector backfill, or sessions of an older plugin version; that is why every Claude Code session must be quit first. Operations that start after `moved.json` exists use the shared store.

After the move the legacy directory stays exactly as it was, plus `moved.json`; you may delete it. Uninstalling the plugin does not touch the moved store, because the shared directory is outside the plugin data directory.

### An existing store in the shared directory

When the shared directory already holds a store, the move refuses and leaves the source unchanged. Move the shared directory aside, run the move again, then rename the aside directory back or delete it:

```bash
mv "$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory" "$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory.aside"
```

To bring the memories of the aside store into the moved one, export them from the aside store and import them after the move:

```bash
ACM_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory.aside" node "<root>/dist/cli.js" export "$HOME/acm-aside.jsonl"
```

```bash
ACM_DATA_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/adaptive-cognitive-memory" node "<root>/dist/cli.js" import "$HOME/acm-aside.jsonl"
```

`export` carries only memories, relations and transitions; the aside store's verdicts, injections, session tables and recall switches stay behind. Run `reembed` afterwards, because imported rows arrive without vectors.

To resume an interrupted move, run the same command again. When `moved.json` points to a directory other than the one `ACM_DATA_DIR` resolves to, Claude Code uses the moved store and its notice names the directory to set `ACM_DATA_DIR` to.

### Roll back the move

The move leaves the legacy store untouched, so a rollback loses nothing. Quit every Claude Code session first, then do one of:

- Keep the pre-move state: delete `moved.json` from the legacy directory. Claude Code then uses the legacy store as it was at the move.
- Keep what was written after the move: with every session on every host quit (so the shared database is checkpointed), remove the legacy `memory.sqlite-wal` and `memory.sqlite-shm`, copy the shared `memory.sqlite` over the legacy `memory.sqlite`, and delete `moved.json`. Or point the older plugin at the shared database with `ACM_DB_PATH=<shared dir>/memory.sqlite`; plugin 0.3.0 honours it and the schema version is unchanged.

Export and import is not a lossless rollback, because export leaves verdicts, injections, session tables and recall switches behind.

The MCP server is named `memory`. Each host prefixes its tools differently: `mcp__plugin_adaptive-cognitive-memory_memory__memory_*` on Claude Code, `mcp__memory__memory_*` on Codex and `memory_memory_*` on OpenCode.

| Tool | Arguments | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `memory_store` | required: `title` (≤200), `content` (≤32000), `type`, `kind`, `conflict_key` (lowercase dotted, ≤120); optional: `cardinality` (`single`\|`multi`, default `multi`), `value_text` (≤200, required for `single`), `keywords` (≤300), `anchors` (≤20 × ≤200), `questions` (≤8 × ≤200: prompts a user would type when the memory matters, in English and the user's language; each one is embedded and recall matches prompts against it), `scope` (`project`\|`user`, default `project`), `abstract`, `resolution` (`{action: ADD\|UPDATE\|SUPERSEDE\|NOOP, target?}`). A `conflict_key` is `namespace.topic` with namespace one of `project`, `build`, `test`, `deploy`, `db`, `api`, `code`, `git`, `tool`, `team`, `user`, `error`, `ticket`, and an anchor is a command head of at most 3 words, a project-relative path, a directory prefix ending in `/`, a basename, an extension, an upper-case ticket id or an error code | `{id, action: created\|superseded\|updated\|noop, refId?, promotedId?}` or `{status: needs_resolution, candidates, allowed}` |
| `memory_search` | `query` (required, may be blank), `limit` (1–100, default 10), `type`, `scope` | `{results: [{id, scope, type, importance, abstract, state, score}], degraded?}`; active and hypothesis memories, never revoked ones |
| `memory_list` | optional filters `state`, `kind`, `type`, `scope`; `before` (the `next_cursor` of the previous page); `limit` (1–50, default 20); `project: "all"` lists every project's memories read-only (never the default; without it only the memories visible to this project) | `{rows: [{id, title, abstract, kind, type, scope, project_id, state, conflict_key, value_text, importance, support_count, injection_count, used_count, wrong_count, valid_from, updated_at}], next_cursor?}`, newest first, never `content`, changing nothing; a page stays within 40,000 characters of JSON, so it can hold fewer rows than `limit`; `next_cursor` is absent on the last page |
| `memory_get` | `id` (full id or unique prefix) | full record incl. `content`, `state`, `conflict_key`, `value_text`, `superseded_by`, `relations` |
| `memory_update` | `id`, plus at least one of `title`, `abstract`, `content`, `keywords`, `anchors`, `questions`; `keywords`, `anchors` and `questions` replace the stored value whole and pass the same checks as `memory_store`; `scope` or `kind` is rejected (store the memory again, then delete the old one) | updated record; revoked memories are immutable |
| `memory_feedback` | `used`, `not_applicable`, `wrong`: lists of ids as recall printed them, 1–20 ids in total, each id under one verdict | `{memories: [{id, state}]}`; `wrong` moves a memory to `hypothesis`, `used` brings it back; a call naming an unknown or revoked id records nothing |
| `memory_delete` | `id` | `{deleted: true}`; deletes the row, its vector and its relations |
| `memory_relate` | `source_id`, `target_id`, `relation_type` (≤40) | `{ok: true}`; rejects self-relations, unknown ids and a 21st relation |
| `memory_status` | none | this project's id and recall switch; memory counts by state × kind for `user` scope and the project; transitions by reason; the share of the newest 500 recall events that injected anything (admission rejections and gate abstentions included), in total and per event (`SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`); the share of memories other than the pinned constraints and preferences injected in receipt-giving sessions that never got `used`; verdict coverage, the share of the newest 500 injections of unpinned memories (one per session and memory) that got an explicit verdict in the same session; the newest 10 open capture signals with session and age; the last 10 injections |
| `memory_doctor` | none | the doctor report |

Invalid input returns `{error: {field, message}}` and persists nothing. An anchor no recall path can match or a `conflict_key` outside `namespace.topic` with a listed namespace is rejected the same way, the message naming the fix; the standard behind these rules is [`skills/memory/references/authoring.md`](../skills/memory/references/authoring.md). Keys are checked as they will be stored: an anchor holding a secret is rejected, because redaction would change it and it could never match, and `keywords` or a `value_text` that redaction would lengthen past its limit are rejected too. When the native module or the database cannot be used, every tool except `memory_doctor` returns an error naming the cause and the fix.

# Memory authoring standard

The server rejects what no recall path can match; its message names the fix. Forms marked (guidance) are not checked.

| Field | Limit | Form | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| title | 200 characters | the lesson in a few words (guidance) | `Run backend tests with uv run pytest -q` | `Note` |
| abstract | 200 characters | the one line recall prints, not the title again (guidance) | `Run uv run pytest -q from the repository root` | the title repeated |
| content | 32000 characters | English, one topic, insight first, then the reason (guidance) | `Tests need Postgres: the ledger uses advisory locks.` | a pasted log |
| conflict_key | 120 characters | `namespace.topic`, lowercase, dotted, namespace from the table below; name the area, not the project (guidance) | `test.command.backend` | `billing.test_command` |
| cardinality + value_text | 200 characters | `single` with the current value in a few words; `multi` when values coexist | `single`, `PostgreSQL 15` | `single` without a value |
| keywords | 300 characters | lower-case terms, each once, identifiers as written (guidance) | `pytest fixtures xdist docker` | `Tests, tests, TESTS` |
| anchors | 20 anchors | each one of the forms below, at most 200 characters, listed once | `pytest`, `billing/tax.py` | `/Users/me/app/billing/tax.py` |
| scope | — | `user` only for what holds in every project; keys are not tied to scope (guidance) | `user` for an editor preference | `user` for one project's database |

## Anchors

An anchor matches exactly what a hook derives before the tool call:

- before Bash, a command head of at most 3 words (`pytest`, `git commit`, `uv run pytest`);
- before Read, Edit or Write, the project-relative path (`billing/tax.py`), a directory prefix ending in `/` (`migrations/versions/`), the basename with or without its extension (`pyproject.toml`, `Dockerfile`) or an extension (`.vue`); an extension fires on every file of that type, so keep it for rules that hold for all of them (guidance);
- an upper-case ticket id as it appears in the branch (`TOUCH-4945`);
- an error code or class name (`ENOENT`, `ModuleNotFoundError`).

A path of more than 3 space-separated words can only be anchored by a directory prefix or its extension.

Good anchors: `pytest` `git commit` `uv run pytest` `go test ./...` `billing/tax.py` `migrations/versions/` `pyproject.toml` `Dockerfile` `.vue` `pages/[id].vue` `TOUCH-4945` `ENOENT` `ModuleNotFoundError`
Bad anchors: `/Users/me/app/billing/tax.py` `./scripts/release.sh` `billing\tax.py` `src/*.ts` `uv run pytest tests/test_tax.py` `touch-4945`
